rv.q: You cannot fault the York Theater Company's rich new production of 'Rothschild & Sons,' a one-act reimagining that looks absolutely royal in the intimate Theater at St. Peter's...
Rothschild & Sons is a strong, sturdy work of musical theater, a rugged dramatization of a now little-known period in European and Jewish history.

What’s left is still often compelling, a haves-vs.-have-nots epic on a small stage, where family squabbles over strategy—should we buy tea or cotton, should we believe Metternich’s promise he’ll dismantle the ghetto walls or not?—take front and center against a larger backdrop of European history.
ROTHSCHILD & SONS is that rare Bock and Harnick musical that never seems to find its heart.
It does not, though, fix -- or "reimagine" -- the show.
Still, even a smoothly professional production can’t hide the doldrums that eventually set in with a disappointingly bland score...
But I would respectfully submit that, if, after seven years, this is the result, then it may be time to move on.
Unfortunately, their new concoction, directed by Jeffrey B. Moss, is a puzzlement to say the least.
Rothschild & Sons, however, is so much on a mission as to be tedious.
The total effect is to make one appreciate anew the special quality of the work.
'Rothschild & Sons' is vigorous, illuminating, fascinating, and moving.
A show well worth seeing for the talent in the production, as well as for the history lesson to be learned on the Rothschild family.
This show is moving and heartwarming.
Where the show falls down is in the music.
In its present form, under the direction of Jeffrey B. Moss, it’s never less than absorbing.
It is a message so strongly delivered that it makes what Harnick, Yellen and Moss have done worth doing.
While the first twenty minutes drag on, when we finally settle in, gravitas and ethos hit hard.
However, it’s still an old tale that has lost its power and feels worn-out.
I can only wish them well in finding a new life for it with this version.
Some projects are worthy of revival but this piece will only appeal to true musical enthusiasts seeking a glimpse of theatre history.
Unfortunately, the current production at the York Theatre is poorly directed by Jeffrey B. Moss with awkward pacing, a lack of focus, and acceptance of some truly awful overacting.

It is this hokum, the cloyingly sentimental portrayal of some sort of do-gooder banking — financiers sans frontiers! — that undercuts the more successful parts of “Rothschild & Sons,” notably Bock’s melodies...

cn.t: Bock and Harnick's final collaboration receives a mixed revival, with critics divided on whether this tale of the Jewish banking dynasty has sufficient emotional resonance beyond its historical interest and solid craftsmanship.
